calls.head: Who drives the play: the Bruins
calls.body: The Bruins have been near the top of the league at controlling the chances at 5-on-5, and the Maple Leafs one of the worst. Expect the Bruins to spend more of the night in the Maple Leafs’ end. That’s about the puck, not the scoreboard: goalies and finishing decide plenty of games the chances don’t.

calls.head: Patience vs. spray-and-pray
calls.body: On shot quality, Boston is one of the league’s best, but Toronto is one of the worst. They’re about as far apart as two teams get. The more dangerous chances are likely to be the Bruins’.
calls.call: The Bruins’ shots are more dangerous on average than the Maple Leafs’.

surprises.head: Boston couldn’t get good looks
surprises.body: Boston usually gets some of the league’s most dangerous shots. Not tonight: a 4.0% chance of scoring on the average shot at 5-on-5, against their usual 6.7% and a league average of 6.3%. A team strays this far about once every 70 games.

story.head: Rielly scores twice as the Maple Leafs beat the Bruins
paras: Morgan Rielly, who scores in about 1 game in 11, scored twice. Casey Mittelstadt opened the scoring for the Bruins on the power play early in the first, but they didn’t score again. The Bruins’ David Pastrňák left in the first period and didn’t return. Rielly tied it 1-1 for Toronto late in the period. Rielly scored his 100th NHL goal late in the second to put the Maple Leafs ahead for good. Colton Sissons stretched the lead to 3-1 early in the third, in his first game back after missing seven games.

The Bruins outshot the Maple Leafs 29-18, but the Maple Leafs’ looks were better, so the chances came out about even. Anthony Stolarz made 28 saves for the Maple Leafs, and Jeremy Swayman stopped 15 of 18 at the other end.

The Maple Leafs killed off a two-man advantage that lasted just under two minutes early in the third. The Leafs improved to 10-14-3, still last in the Atlantic, while the Bruins fell to 15-9-1, slipping to fifth in the Atlantic.
